references.text: Earlier, Luke tells us that the chief priests and the scribes sought to get Jesus out of the way, but they feared the people – the same motive as in 20:19. See [ref:Luk 19:47-48|Luke 19:47-48].
The chief priests and the scribes continued to look for a way to seize Jesus, which is a direct continuation of the conflict in 20:19. See [ref:Luk 22:2|Luke 22:2].
The parallel passage in Mark tells us that they understood the parable was directed at them, and they wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd. See [ref:Mark 12:12|Mark 12:12].

The parallel passage in Matthew tells us that the chief priests and the Pharisees understood that Jesus was speaking about them in the parable, and that they wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd. See [ref:Matt 21:45-46|Matthew 21:45-46].
The parable of the wicked tenants that Jesus had just told, which the chief priests and the scribes understood was directed at them. See [ref:Luk 20:9-18|Luke 20:9-18].

Also in John's Gospel they sought to seize Jesus, but no one laid hands on him because his hour had not yet come – a similar pattern of attempts to arrest him that were thwarted. See [ref:Joh 7:30|John 7:30].

Some wanted to seize Jesus, but no one laid hands on him – the people's response and God's providence protected him, parallel to the situation in [ref:Luk 20:19|Luke 20:19]. See [ref:Joh 7:44|John 7:44].
The chief priests and the scribes challenged Jesus' authority earlier in the chapter, which is the background for the hostile reaction in verse 19. See [ref:Luk 20:1-2|Luke 20:1-2].
Already early in Jesus' ministry, the scribes and Pharisees became furious and began to discuss what they could do with Jesus – the same hostile motive as in 20:19. See [ref:Luk 6:11|Luke 6:11].
